requirements.title: One record per check

statements.text:
`judge-jev check` MUST take one of two argument forms: a single record
with a location and a mode, or a `--profile`.

In the single-record form, `judge-jev check` MUST take one record id,
given with exactly one record-kind flag: `--req` (requirement), `--adr`
(architecture decision record) or `--nfr` (non-functional requirement).

In the single-record form, `judge-jev check` MUST take exactly one
`--location`.

In the single-record form, `judge-jev check` MUST take exactly one
`--mode`.
Each record kind MUST use its own question set.

requirements.rationale:
A requirement, a decision and a non-functional requirement are each
violated in a different way.

acceptance_criteria.text:
The same location checked with `--req` and with `--adr` sends
different question sets.

requirements.title: One record and one location per request

statements.text: Each Jev request MUST carry exactly one record.
Each Jev request MUST carry exactly one location.
A run over many pairs MUST send them as a stream of single requests.

requirements.rationale:
Jev judges one record and location at a time; packing records into one request hides
which one failed. Batching is streaming single requests, which the batch
command already does.

acceptance_criteria.text: A profile mapping one file to three records sends three requests.

requirements.title: Target modes

statements.text: judge-jev MUST support the target mode `prompt`.
judge-jev MUST support the target mode `skill`.
judge-jev MUST support the target mode `task`.
judge-jev MUST support the target mode `code`.
In `task` mode judge-jev MUST judge the raw template.

In `task` mode judge-jev MUST judge an assignment rendered by sc-compose
in strict mode from the vars file that `--vars` names, or, in a profile
run, that the profile names.

In `code` mode judge-jev MUST resolve the location with the tree-sitter
grammars sc-agent defines.
judge-jev MUST NOT define its own tree-sitter grammars.

requirements.rationale:
The raw template shows which variables are substituted; a rendered
assignment shows what an agent actually receives. Strict rendering fails on
a missing variable instead of judging a half-rendered assignment. sc-agent
owns the grammars so every consumer selects code the same way.

acceptance_criteria.text:
A task template checked in `task` mode produces one result for the
raw template and one for its rendered assignment.

A vars file missing a template variable fails the render with the
variable named.
The repository contains no tree-sitter grammar definitions.

implementation_notes.text: `code` mode waits for sc-agent's tree-sitter grammars (ADR-JEV-0004).

requirements.title: Profiles map locations to records

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST read a TOML profile listing locations, each with its
mode, the record ids that govern it, and for `task` mode a vars file.
`judge-jev check --profile <profile>` MUST check every listed pair.
`judge-jev check --profile <profile>` MUST report each pair's verdict.

`judge-jev check --profile <profile>` MUST aggregate the verdicts per
record.

`judge-jev check --profile <profile>` MUST aggregate the verdicts per
location.
A profile run MUST NOT judge a pair the profile does not list.

requirements.rationale:
The profile states which records govern which locations, so a run checks
exactly those pairs. A record id carries its kind, so one profile holds
all kinds.

acceptance_criteria.text:
A run over a profile produces one result per (record, location)
pair and none for unlisted pairs.

The report states, per record, whether it is met at every listed
location, and names the failing locations.

requirements.title: Question sets ship with the tool

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST ship one question set per combination of record kind and
target class (agent text or code).
judge-jev MUST ship one quality decision tree per record kind.

Every shipped question and prompt text MUST be approved by Rand before
it ships.
Question sets MUST be data files shipped with the tool.
Quality decision trees MUST be data files shipped with the tool.
The released tool MUST accept an override file for any question set.

The released tool MUST accept an override file for any quality decision
tree.
Every result MUST carry the question-set id.
Every result MUST carry the content digest of the file used.
Every log entry MUST carry the question-set id.
Every log entry MUST carry the content digest of the file used.

requirements.rationale:
Rand: "I do not trust non-frontier agents to write prompts. I do not even
trust frontier agents to write them." The question sets are the tool's
system prompts. Getting them production-worthy means running thousands of
question variations against the released tool; a variation that needs a
code change cannot be run at that scale.

Because question sets and trees are data files, changing a question, a
tree branch or a wave needs no code change. An override file lets a
variation be tried by writing a file, never by changing or rebuilding code.
The question-set id and file digest on every result and log entry let
results from many variations of the same set be told apart and compared.

acceptance_criteria.text: Each shipped question file names the approval that admitted its text.

A result produced with an override names the override file and its
digest.

Two override files differing in one question produce results with
different digests, run on the same released build.
Adding a wave to a quality tree changes only the tree file.

requirements.title: One judgment per record and location

statements.text:
When a record is satisfied in more than one location (prompt, skill,
agent, template or code), judge-jev MUST judge the record separately at
each location.
judge-jev MUST report one result per (record, location) pair.
judge-jev MUST NOT combine a record's locations into one judgment.

requirements.rationale:
Rand (2026-11-07): "from raptor config standpoint for judge-jev, we must
have single requirements mapped to multiple places in
prompts/skills/agents/code I would expect a separate jev query for each
location it is satisfied. We may be able to fan out a single jev call w/
<location> - <question-1-req-1> | <question-2-req-1> | <question-3-req-2>
| <question-4-req-2> | ... depending on how we can fit items in context"
Rand (2026-11-08): "batching is simply streaming of single requests."

acceptance_criteria.text:
A record mapped to three locations produces three results, one per
location.
A failure at one location is reported against that location only.

requirements.title: Location syntax

statements.text:
A location MUST take one of three forms: `path`, `path#Heading` or
`path::Symbol`.
A `path` location MUST select the whole file.

A `path#Heading` location MUST select a Markdown section, from the
heading to the next heading of the same or higher level.

A `path::Symbol` location MUST select a code symbol resolved by
sc-agent's tree-sitter grammars.

Markdown sections MUST be parsed by the same rules Raptor uses for the
same file.
A location MUST NOT be a line range.

requirements.rationale:
Line ranges drift on every edit; headings and symbols survive. One
Markdown parsing rule keeps judge-jev and Raptor agreeing on what a
section is.

acceptance_criteria.text:
`path#Heading` selects the same text Raptor attributes to that
heading.

A heading or symbol that does not resolve is a typed error naming the
location.

implementation_notes.text:
Open: which Raptor parser and heading rules judge-jev matches, and whether
paths in a profile are relative to the profile or to the repository root.

requirements.title: Dry run audits the composed request

statements.text: `judge-jev quality` MUST accept `--dry-run`.
`judge-jev check` MUST accept `--dry-run`.
A dry run MUST compose every request without calling Jev.
Each dry-run entry MUST report the record id.
Each dry-run entry MUST report the record's Raptor source.

Each dry-run entry MUST report the resolved location as its path, section
or symbol.

Each dry-run entry MUST report the digest of the location's selected
text.
Each dry-run entry MUST report the mode.

Each dry-run entry MUST report the question set as its shipped id or its
override path.
In `task` mode, each dry-run entry MUST report the vars file.
In `task` mode, each dry-run entry MUST report the rendered text.
Each dry-run entry MUST report the full composed request.

Each dry-run entry MUST report the composed request's size against the
request limit.
For `quality`, the dry run MUST report the decision tree.
For `quality`, the dry run MUST report the composed wave-1 request.

A dry run MUST fail with a typed error on anything that would make the
live request wrong: an unresolved record or location, a render failure,
or an oversize request.

requirements.rationale:
The caller must know the prompt will be built correctly before any text
leaves the machine. A `quality` dry run stops at wave 1 because later
waves depend on live answers.

acceptance_criteria.text:
A dry run makes no network call and reports one entry per request a
live run would send.

A dry run over a task location with a missing variable fails naming
the variable.

requirements.title: Record quality command

statements.text: `judge-jev quality` MUST take one or more record ids.

`judge-jev quality` MUST take each record id with one record-kind flag:
`--req` (requirement), `--adr` (architecture decision record) or `--nfr`
(non-functional requirement).
Every record-kind flag of `judge-jev quality` MUST be repeatable.

`judge-jev quality` MUST judge each record with its kind's quality
decision tree (REQ-JEV-0101).

All records of one `judge-jev quality` invocation MUST be logged under
one run name.

requirements.rationale:
Quality and compliance are separate questions about separate inputs. One
run name per invocation groups a measurement over many records in the
log.

acceptance_criteria.text:
Every request `judge-jev quality --req <id>` sends carries only the
record and questions from the REQ quality tree.

requirements.title: Validate command

statements.text: `judge-jev validate` MUST take one input file.

`judge-jev validate` MUST take one input-kind flag with that file:
`--tree` (quality tree), `--questions` (question set), `--answers`
(answers file), `--index` (Raptor import index) or `--requests` (batch
request stream).

`judge-jev validate` MUST check the file with the model `judge-jev`
applies to that input kind before its first Jev request (ADR-JEV-0005).
Every refusal from `judge-jev validate` MUST name the field path.

Every refusal from `judge-jev validate` MUST name the rule the field
breaks.

`judge-jev validate --answers` MUST apply the answers-file envelope that
`--answers-file` applies before the first request.
The answers-file envelope MUST require an object of string keys.

The answers-file envelope MUST require each key's value to be an object
or a non-empty list of objects.

The answers-file envelope MUST require an object with `__error__` to hold
only a string code of at most 64 characters.
`judge-jev validate` MUST NOT call Jev.

requirements.rationale:
A tree variation checked before a run costs nothing; one refused after a
paid call wastes it.

The answers file stands in for Jev's response, so what an answer holds
(its questions, choices and probabilities) is not part of the envelope; it
is checked after the send as `JEV.RESPONSE_INVALID`.

acceptance_criteria.text:
Every input the sweep tests refuse in `quality` is refused by
`judge-jev validate` with the same field path.
The shipped trees and question sets pass `judge-jev validate`.

requirements.title: A typed result for every input

statements.text:
For every input, every `judge-jev` command MUST print exactly one JSON
object.

The JSON object a `judge-jev` command prints MUST be its result or a
typed error.

`judge-jev` MUST refuse an invalid tree, question set, index, request
stream or run directory before its first Jev request.

`judge-jev` MUST check that every log event of a request (the request,
Jev's largest possible answer and the result) fits the logger's event
size limit before sending the request.

requirements.rationale:
Rand Lee, 2026-11-08: "Crash is not acceptable for any input." A refusal
after a paid call wastes the call; a crash loses its answer.

acceptance_criteria.text:
The sweep tests (every field of a tree, index and answers file
replaced by each of a fixed list of wrong values, deleted or given an
extra key, and raw JSON no value expresses) produce no `SCRIPT.INTERNAL`
and no refusal after a request is sent.
Invalid UTF-8 on stdin is refused with `INPUT.MALFORMED`.

requirements.title: Targeted definitions

statements.text:
A definition MUST be attachable to a record alone, or to a record and
one location under evaluation.

A request about a record MUST carry, in its state next to the record, only
the definitions attached to that record alone, plus those attached to
that record and the request's location.

A request with no matching definition MUST be identical to the request
sent without definitions.

`judge-jev` MUST refuse, before sending, a request whose definitions take
it over the size limit.

Every request's log event MUST record the digest of each definition it
carried.
`judge-jev` MUST NOT truncate a definition.

requirements.rationale:
Rand Lee, 2026-11-08: "we can NOT write a single definition file and add it
to every prompt" when running over 1000 to 2000 records with 1 to 200
locations each. A record-only definition "makes the req/nfr/adr w/ confusing
term carry the definition w/ it for all jev calls"; a record-and-location
definition "would only be added to specific data (code/prompt/skill) which
requires clarification".

acceptance_criteria.text:
With definitions linked to record A only, the requests for record B
are byte-identical to a run without definitions.

The requests for record A carry exactly A's definitions, and their log
events list those definitions' digests.

A definition attached to record A and location X is carried by A's
request for X and by no other request about A.

requirements.title: A definition is kept only when it changes an answer

statements.text:
`judge-jev` MUST provide a comparison of one or more candidate
definitions.

The comparison MUST run the requests the candidate definitions would
reach with the candidates.
The comparison MUST run the same requests without the candidates.

The comparison MUST report each answer's choice with and without the
candidates.

The comparison MUST report each answer's confidence with and without the
candidates.

The comparison MUST report the candidates as material when an answer's
choice flips or its confidence crosses the decision threshold, and as not
material when every change stays on the same side of the threshold.
The comparison MUST record the threshold it applied.

requirements.rationale:
Rand Lee, 2026-11-08: "if adding the definition does not impact the scores
used in the rubric, they aren't necessary to add"; "Moving from 90->95
confidence doesn't matter. A change from 20%->50% would be material if
other changes get it over the threshold."

acceptance_criteria.text:
With fixture answers where the definition flips one answer, the
comparison reports it as material.

With fixture answers that are the same with and without the
definition, the comparison reports it as not material.

A confidence move from 0.90 to 0.95 on the same side of the threshold
is not material. Two candidates that each move an answer part of the way,
and together across the threshold, are material when compared together.

requirements.title: Question ids are unique within a scope

statements.text:
Every question IRI in one scope (by default the repository) MUST be
declared in one tree file only, across judge-jev's trees and every
consumer extension's.

Every `jj:id` in judge-jev's trees and in every consumer extension's
MUST be unique within its tree.

requirements.rationale:
A question's identity is its IRI.

Rand Lee, 2026-11-08: "We would need to make sure all questions in
judge-jev AND in consumer extensions follow a naming policy for uniqueness
w/in that scope (repo is typical scope)."

acceptance_criteria.text:
A question IRI declared in two tree files of one scope is reported
as an error naming both files; two questions of one tree with the same
`jj:id` are an error.

requirements.title: Doctor command

statements.text:
`judge-jev doctor` MUST validate every tree in the scope against its
schema.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST validate every question set in the scope against
its schema.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST validate every definitions file in the scope
against its schema.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST validate every tree, question set and definitions
file in the scope against the ontology's shapes, including edges and
cycles.
`judge-jev doctor` MUST report each validation failure as an error.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST report a definition with no attachment as a
warning.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST report an attachment to a record the Raptor index
does not hold as a warning.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST report an attachment to a location that does not
exist as a warning.

`judge-jev doctor` MUST report a definition whose source does not exist
as a warning.
`judge-jev doctor` MUST NOT call Jev.
A `judge-jev doctor` warning MUST NOT fail the command.

requirements.rationale:
Rand Lee, 2026-11-08: "I would expect judge-jev doctor to report orphans/dead
links as warnings, it would also run schema validation and verify ontology
followed and no cycles."

acceptance_criteria.text: A scope with one orphan definition exits 0 with one warning naming it.

A scope with a tree that has a cycle exits non-zero with an error
naming the cycle.

requirements.title: Records come from Raptor

statements.text: judge-jev MUST obtain records through Raptor's query interface.
judge-jev MUST NOT parse record Markdown itself.

judge-jev MUST NOT run SQL (Structured Query Language) against the record
store itself.

requirements.rationale:
Raptor owns the schema and every conversion; the Raptor team can change
them and notify judge-jev without breaking it.

acceptance_criteria.text: judge-jev contains no Markdown record parser and no SQL statement.

requirements.title: One batch command calls Jev

statements.text: judge-jev MUST send every Jev request through one batch command.
The batch command MUST read request lines.
The batch command MUST write one result envelope per request.
The batch command MUST use typed error codes.
The batch command MUST apply a fixed retry policy.
The batch command MUST enforce request size limits.

The batch command MUST log every request through the sc-observability
logger (REQ-JEV-0008).

The batch command MUST log every answer through the sc-observability
logger (REQ-JEV-0008).

requirements.rationale:
One call path keeps the Jev core stable while a Rust implementation
replaces it (ADR-JEV-0001).

acceptance_criteria.text:
A request file of three lines produces three result envelopes and
three log entries.

requirements.title: TypeSafe key lookup

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST read the TypeSafe API key from `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` first,
then from the platform credential store, service `plan-anchor`, account
`typesafe-api-key`.

requirements.rationale: Tools that call Jev share one stored key, saved once.

acceptance_criteria.text:
A key stored under that service and account is found with no other
setup.

requirements.title: Remote-judge consent

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST refuse every live Jev call with
`POLICY.REMOTE_JUDGE_DISABLED` unless the committed
`.sc/judge-jev/settings.yaml` sets `allow_remote_judge: true`.
judge-jev MUST NOT write that setting without the user's answer.

requirements.rationale: Text sent to Jev leaves the machine; the user decides once per repository.

acceptance_criteria.text:
With the setting absent or false, a live call exits with
`POLICY.REMOTE_JUDGE_DISABLED` and sends nothing.

requirements.title: Marketplace and installer

statements.text: judge-jev MUST ship as a marketplace plugin for Claude.
judge-jev MUST ship as a marketplace plugin for Codex.
judge-jev MUST ship as a marketplace plugin for Cursor.
An upgrade MUST update every harness that is locked, installed or present.

requirements.rationale: No harness is left on an old version.

acceptance_criteria.text:
Upgrading in a repository with Claude, Codex and Cursor installs
updates all three.

requirements.title: Local record database built through Raptor

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST obtain its record database by asking Raptor to build a
local SQLite database from the repository's Raptor-parseable Markdown on
each run.

When Raptor supplies a SQLite snapshot of a Dolt branch, judge-jev MUST
query it through the same Raptor interface.

requirements.rationale:
Querying SQLite is the same work whether it was built from Markdown or
pulled from Dolt, so the source can change without changing judge-jev.

acceptance_criteria.text:
A run in a repository with a `.raptor/` configuration judges records
from a database built in that run.

requirements.title: judge-jev's own records are Raptor-parseable

statements.text:
judge-jev's requirements, non-functional requirements and decisions MUST
import through Raptor with no issues.

requirements.rationale:
judge-jev depends on Raptor's format, so its own records prove the format
first.

acceptance_criteria.text: Raptor's import of this repository reports zero issues.

requirements.title: Logging through the sc-observability logger

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST write its run logs (requests, answers, quality-tree
branches, verdicts) through the sc-observability logger, the logger
sc-agent uses.
judge-jev MUST NOT keep its own log format alongside it.

requirements.rationale:
Rand (2026-11-08): "we will need to use sc-observability logger for both
(this is what sc-agent uses). we should implement in judge-jev first then
we can upgrade plan-anchor which is currently working solidly."

acceptance_criteria.text:
A live `check` run's requests, answers and verdicts appear in the
sc-observability log.
No judge-jev command writes `anchor-runs/tournament-*.jsonl`.

implementation_notes.text:
Today the copied core writes its own `anchor-runs/tournament-<run>.jsonl`
(`jev_judge.py` `pump_batch`). plan-anchor moves to the same logger after
judge-jev.

requirements.title: Deterministic offline tests

statements.text: judge-jev tests MUST run offline against recorded Jev answers.
judge-jev tests MUST NOT depend on timing.
judge-jev tests MUST NOT depend on sleeps.
judge-jev tests MUST NOT depend on ordering.

requirements.rationale:
Flaky tests are prohibited; live Jev calls are neither free nor
repeatable.

acceptance_criteria.text: The test suite passes 20 consecutive runs with networking disabled.

requirements.title: Record quality mode

statements.text:
judge-jev MUST provide a mode that reports, for one requirement (REQ),
non-functional requirement (NFR) or architecture decision record (ADR),
the verdict of that record kind's quality decision tree.

The mode MUST judge only records that Raptor imported without
diagnostics.

The mode MUST run as a decision tree of prompts: each wave sends several
questions, and the answers to one wave select the next wave's questions.

Every wave MUST report, as its reason, each of its questions with the
question's id and text, Jev's choice and Jev's confidence.

A wave the tree marks per statement MUST send one request for each MUST
and MUST NOT statement of the record, carrying that statement with the
whole record as context.

A per-statement wave's reason MUST list each statement's index and text
with each question's id, choice and confidence.

A per-statement wave's verdict rule MUST be able to fire when any one
statement's answers match it.

A per-statement wave's verdict MUST name the statements whose answers
fired its rule.

A per-statement request that gets no answer MUST fail with an error that
names its statement.
A wave after the first MUST refine the answers of the wave before it.

A wave after the first MUST be designed from the observed live results
of the wave before it.

A wave with no next wave MUST end the walk, with its verdict given by a
rule in the tree file over that wave's answers.

The tree MUST ship with the tool as a data file a consumer can override
(REQ-JEV-0205); answers select the branch and the verdict, never a model
choosing the next questions.
A failing answer MUST report the decision-tree path that failed.

A live run MUST log every wave as output: its composed request, Jev's
answers, its reason and the branch or verdict they selected.
The mode MUST NOT check structure that Raptor's import checks.

requirements.rationale:
Importing is part of complying with the schema: Raptor's import
diagnostics (REQ-RAP-0012) bring a document into the schema, then this
mode judges whether each imported record is well written. Prose evaluation
uses only records that pass both.

Rand (2026-11-08): "for the 'is this adr/nfr/req high quality' mode, I
would expect this to be a decision tree of prompts. each layer of the tree
would output several questions which based on the wave-1 outputs would
result in a new set of questions to narrow in." On a dry run showing only
wave 1: "as long as real run logs all info as output (sc-agent will do logging and is
almost ready to start testing)."

Rand (2026-11-08), after the first live run reported only fixed leaf text:
"every wave needs to provide some 'reason' the next wave is just to refine
it. You can't design wave-2 until you see wave-1 results so you know what
wave-2 should ask." The shipped trees therefore hold wave 1 only; a wave 2
is designed from wave 1's observed answers.

Rand (2026-11-08) approved per-statement waves: one request per MUST / MUST
NOT statement, with that statement plus the whole record as context, so a
failure names the statement to fix.

acceptance_criteria.text: Fixed answers to a wave select the same next wave every run.

Every wave's result lists each of its questions with id, text,
choice and confidence.

A live run's log holds each wave's request, answers, reason and
selected branch or verdict.

A REQ with two MUST statements and one SHOULD statement sends two
wave-1 requests, one per MUST statement.

A REQ whose third statement answers `check: none` reports `no`, names
statement 3, and lists every statement's answers in wave 1's reason.
A dry run shows the composed wave-1 request for every statement.
A record Raptor rejected is not sent to Jev.

implementation_notes.text:
Logging goes through the sc-observability logger (REQ-JEV-0008). A
per-statement node sets `"per": "statement"`, `statements` (the record
field holding the statements) and `modals` (the modals judged); each
statement is one request whose item text is `{statement, record}`. The
shipped REQ and NFR trees ask, per statement, `obligations`, `joined_by`,
`term` and `check`; the ADR tree asks, per record, `context`,
`alternatives` and `consequences`. Each option's criterion carries its fix
hint, and the reason reports it.

decisions.title: Keep the Jev core unchanged until its Rust replacement

context.text:
judge-jev's Jev core (the batch command, request and result contracts,
key lookup and remote-judge consent) is copied from an existing
implementation, and a Rust implementation, exposed through PyO3 bindings or
a command-line interface (CLI), will replace that Python core. The problem
is whether the Python core may change before then: any change to its
architecture or contracts is a change the Rust replacement must reproduce,
or its callers break when the replacement lands.

decision.text:
The Jev core keeps its architecture and contracts unchanged. It changes
only to fix a defect, or to replace its run log with the sc-observability
logger (REQ-JEV-0008).

rationale.text:
An unchanged core lets the Rust implementation replace it with no change
to its callers.

positive: The Rust replacement is a drop-in.
negative: Improvements to the core wait for the Rust implementation.

groups.name: Improve the Python core before the Rust replacement
groups.description: Change the copied core's architecture or contracts now.
groups.why_rejected:
The Rust implementation could then not replace the core
without a change to its callers.

decisions.title: Query records through Raptor over local SQLite

context.text:
judge-jev needs requirement records to judge, and their source is
changing: requirements move from Markdown files to a Dolt server as the
single source of truth, with the Raptor command-line interface (CLI) as
the access path. Raptor owns the record schema and every conversion
(REQ-JEV-0001). The problem is how judge-jev reads records so that neither
the move to Dolt nor a Raptor schema change breaks it.

decision.text:
judge-jev reads records only through Raptor, which queries a local SQLite
database: built on the fly from Markdown now, pulled from a Dolt branch
later.

rationale.text:
Querying SQLite is the same work either way, so the source can change
without touching judge-jev.

positive: The move to Dolt does not change judge-jev.
negative:
judge-jev depends on Raptor's query contract; Raptor notifies judge-jev
maintenance before changing it.

groups.name: Parse record Markdown directly
groups.description: judge-jev reads the record Markdown files itself.
groups.why_rejected:
Raptor owns the schema and every conversion; a parser in
judge-jev breaks when Raptor changes them (REQ-JEV-0001).

groups.name: Query the record store with SQL directly
groups.description: judge-jev runs its own SQL against the record store.
groups.why_rejected:
Raptor owns the schema; judge-jev's own queries break when
Raptor changes it (REQ-JEV-0001).

decisions.title: Judge record quality instead of loosening the schema

context.text:
Raptor rejects records missing required sections, such as statements
written as plain prose, so corpora with prose-only records do not import.
judge-jev can judge only records with typed statements and criteria. The
problem is how such records get into a judgeable form: by loosening
Raptor's schema to accept them, or by keeping it strict and explaining
what to fix.

decision.text:
Raptor's schema stays strict. Raptor's import diagnostics explain why a
record does not fit the schema; judge-jev's quality mode then explains why
an imported record is not well written.

rationale.text:
An explained rejection gets the document fixed; a looser schema stores
records that cannot be judged.

positive: Every record judge-jev uses has typed statements and criteria.
negative:
Corpora with prose-only records need editing before import, guided by
the import diagnostics.

groups.name: Loosen Raptor's schema
groups.description:
Accept records missing required sections, such as
prose-only statements.
groups.why_rejected: A looser schema stores records that cannot be judged.

decisions.title: Code references are outside the first version

context.text:
Records will eventually govern code as well as prompts, but selecting code
needs tree-sitter grammars, which sc-agent defines and which may not be
complete yet. The problem is what the first version judges while those
grammars are unfinished.

decision.text:
The first version judges prompts, skills and task templates only. Code
references come later through tree-sitter grammars that sc-agent defines;
judge-jev never defines its own grammars. sc-agent's grammars may not be
complete yet.

rationale.text:
Prompt and task wording is the immediate risk; code selection needs the
tree-sitter work first.

positive: The first version ships without a code-reference model.
negative: Code is not judged until the tree-sitter extension exists.

groups.name: judge-jev defines its own tree-sitter grammars
groups.description: Ship grammars inside judge-jev so code is judged now.
groups.why_rejected:
sc-agent owns the grammars so every consumer selects code
the same way (REQ-JEV-0203).

groups.name: Line-range locations for code
groups.description: Reference code by file line ranges instead of symbols.
groups.why_rejected:
Line ranges drift on every edit; symbols survive
(REQ-JEV-0207).

decisions.title: Pydantic models validate every JSON input

context.text:
judge-jev reads JSON written by people and agents (quality trees, question
sets, answers files, request streams), by Raptor (the import index) and by
Jev (responses). Quality trees will be varied thousands of times
(REQ-JEV-0205). Hand-written type checks let fourteen input shapes crash
the script or fail only after a paid Jev call, found by review of PRs #13
and #14. The problem is how to make every input either accepted, or refused
with the exact field, before the first call.

decision.text:
Every JSON input is parsed into a pydantic v2 model in strict mode before
it is used, and code after parsing receives model instances, not
dictionaries. Each model is the single definition of its input's shape.
Rules that span fields (a rule's choices are options of its question, a
`goto` names a node, no cycle, a final rule without conditions) are model
validators. `judge-jev validate` (REQ-JEV-0210) runs the same models
without calling Jev. The JSON shapes of the Jev core's contracts do not
change (ADR-JEV-0001); only how they are checked does.

rationale.text:
One model per input replaces scattered checks that each had to anticipate
every wrong type, and pydantic reports the field path of every refusal.

positive: Every refusal names the field and the rule it breaks.
Tree authors check a variation with `judge-jev validate` before a run.
negative:
pydantic (with its compiled core) becomes a dependency, pinned in the
script's PEP 723 header and in CI.

groups.name: Keep hand-written checks
groups.description: Extend the `isinstance` checks for each new crash found.
groups.why_rejected:
Each new shape needs a new check; review of #13 and #14
found fourteen that were missed.

groups.name: JSON Schema validated by `jsonschema`
groups.description: One schema file per input, validated at load.
groups.why_rejected:
Rules that span fields stay hand-written, and code after
validation still handles untyped dictionaries.

decisions.title: Quality trees and their answers are an RDF graph

context.text:
A quality tree is a graph: waves, questions, options and rules, with edges
between them. As JSON, a question shared by two trees or two waves is
copied, list position carries rule priority, and every structural check is
code judge-jev maintains. Answers live in log files apart from the questions
that produced them, so comparing thousands of question variations means
scraping logs. The problem is how to represent trees and answers so that
questions are shared, structure is checked by existing tools, and every
verdict can be traced through its answers to the exact question and option.

decision.text:
Quality trees are written in Turtle (TTL) against a judge-jev ontology:
waves, questions, options and rules are resources linked by edges, and a
question is one resource with an IRI that any wave may use. Order is a
`rank` property: rules are tried by rank and the reason lists questions by
rank; questions within a wave are otherwise unordered. SHACL shapes over the
ontology validate the graph and its edges (each rule's choices are options
of its question, each `goto` names a node, no cycle, a final rule without
conditions). Pydantic models (ADR-JEV-0005) validate each node's body,
including the per-wave JSON compiled from the graph and sent to Jev. Runs,
answers, fired rules and verdicts are recorded as triples linked to the
questions, options and Raptor records they concern, in an Oxigraph store
(`pyoxigraph` in judge-jev). A tree's digest is the SHA-256 of its
canonical form (RDFC-1.0).

The vocabulary, prefix `jj: <urn:judge-jev:ontology#>`:

- Tree: `jj:Tree` (`jj:start`, `jj:node`, `jj:kind`), `jj:Wave`
  (`jj:asks` a `jj:Question`, `jj:rule`, `jj:per`, `jj:statements`,
  `jj:modal`), `jj:Leaf` (`jj:verdict`).
- Question: `jj:Question` (`jj:instructions`, `jj:option` a `jj:Option`,
  `jj:rank`), `jj:Option` (`jj:label`, `jj:criterion`).
- Rule: `jj:BranchRule` (`jj:goto`) and `jj:VerdictRule` (`jj:verdict`),
  each with `jj:rank` and `jj:whenAll` / `jj:whenAny` a `jj:Condition`
  (`jj:question`, `jj:choice` an `jj:Option`).
- Run: `jj:Run` (`jj:tree`, `jj:treeDigest`, `jj:record` the Raptor
  record's IRI), `jj:WaveRun` (`jj:inRun`, `jj:node`, `jj:requestId`,
  `jj:statement`, `jj:fired` a rule), `jj:Answer` (`jj:ofWaveRun`,
  `jj:toQuestion`, `jj:chose` an `jj:Option`, `jj:confidence`,
  `jj:probability` a `jj:OptionProbability` with `jj:option` and `jj:p`),
  `jj:verdictValue` on a run.

rationale.text:
Validation of the graph moves to SHACL and of node bodies to pydantic, so
judge-jev's own checking code shrinks to the compile step. One graph of
records, questions and answers makes any verdict traceable and any two
question variations comparable with one query.

positive: A question is written once and used by IRI.
A query over the graph compares question variations across runs.
The graph renders in a graph viewer for authoring and diagnosis.

The Rust Jev tool in sc-agent can process the same ontology with
Oxigraph.
negative: `pyoxigraph` and a SHACL validator become dependencies.
Each wave needs a compile step from the graph to Jev's JSON request.
Tree authors write Turtle instead of JSON.

groups.name: JSON trees with references to shared question files
groups.description: Keep JSON; a wave lists `$ref`s that judge-jev resolves.
groups.why_rejected:
It removes duplication only; structure checks stay in
judge-jev's code, and answers stay apart from questions.

groups.name: JSON trees as today
groups.description: Keep one JSON file per tree with inline questions.
groups.why_rejected:
Questions are copied, priority is list position, and
answers cannot be joined to questions without scraping logs.

decisions.title: The seam to sc-agent's Jev tool

context.text:
sc-agent's Rust Jev tool will replace judge-jev's Python Jev core
(ADR-JEV-0001). Its first version will not include Oxigraph, though a later
one may. Quality trees and their answers become an RDF graph
(ADR-JEV-0006). The problem is where the boundary lies, so that judge-jev
works with a Jev tool that has no graph store today, and one with Oxigraph
later takes over graph work without judge-jev changing its callers.

decision.text:
judge-jev has two ports:

- **Transport:** sends the request lines of one wave and returns their
  result lines. Its contract is the existing batch request and result
  schemas (`assets/schemas/jev-batch-request.schema.json`,
  `jev-batch-result.schema.json`), unchanged. The Python core implements it
  now; sc-agent's Jev tool implements it later.
- **Graph store:** loads a tree, validates it with SHACL, compiles a wave
  to its JSON questions, records a run's triples and answers queries.
  judge-jev implements it now with `pyoxigraph` and a SHACL validator; a
  Jev tool with Oxigraph may implement it later.

Only JSON crosses the transport. The result lines in the sc-observability
log are the record of a run; a run's triples are a projection of those
lines and the tree, so they can be rebuilt from the log at any time. The
tree walk (which wave next, which verdict) uses only the compiled waves and
the answers, so it runs on either side of the seam.

rationale.text:
A Jev tool without a graph store needs only the JSON contract it already
has. Because the triples are rebuilt from the log, no run is lost when the
store moves to the other side of the seam.

positive: sc-agent's first Jev tool replaces the Python core with no graph work.

Moving the graph store into sc-agent changes the port's implementation,
not its callers.
negative: Until sc-agent hosts the store, judge-jev carries the graph dependencies.

The projection from result lines to triples must stay in step with the
ontology.

groups.name: sc-agent's Jev tool reads trees and writes triples
groups.description:
Send the TTL tree and the record; the tool walks the tree
and stores the triples.
groups.why_rejected:
Its first version has no graph store, so judge-jev would
wait for it.

groups.name: Triples as the only record of a run
groups.description: Write runs to the graph store instead of the log.
groups.why_rejected:
A tool without a store could not record a run, and a lost
store loses the runs.

decisions.title: Definitions are graph nodes targeted at records

context.text:
A record can use a term that neither the record nor anything Jev sees
defines, and Jev then has to guess. judge-jev runs over 1000 to 2000 REQ,
ADR and NFR records, each with 1 to 200 code locations. A single definitions
file prepended to every request would be sent tens of thousands of times,
almost always to requests that do not need it. Unrelated material lowers
Jev's accuracy and uses up the request budget. The problem is how to supply
a definition only where it changes an answer, and how to find definitions
that no longer serve anything.

decision.text:
A definition is a node in the judge-jev graph (ADR-JEV-0006):

- **`jj:Definition`** holds a `jj:term`, a `jj:text` (short, one line on
  average) and a `jj:source`, the repository file or record that the
  meaning comes from. Pydantic validates the body (ADR-JEV-0005), and SHACL
  validates the edges.
- **`jj:attachedTo`** links a definition to one or more attachments. Each
  attachment names one record (`jj:record`, its Raptor IRI) and optionally
  one location (`jj:location`, the code, prompt, skill or task template
  under evaluation). That gives two cases:
  - **Record only:** the record carries the definition into every Jev call
    about it, every question and every location. Use this when the record's
    own wording is the confusing part.
  - **Record and location:** the definition is added only when that record
    is checked against that location. Use this when the location's material
    needs the clarification, not the record.

  Every question of a request sees its definitions. An attachment is a node
  because an RDF edge links only two things.
- **Storage:** definitions are Turtle files committed in the repository
  under `.sc/judge-jev/`. The per-requirement tree-sitter queries will be
  kept there too, keyed by the same record IDs. Both may move into the
  Raptor database later, once real runs show the feature earns schema
  space. The files load into the store as their own named graph, so they
  never change a tree's digest.

- **Request:** a Jev request has two parts, the state (data) and the
  questions, and Jev answers every question in parallel against the same
  state. Definitions are data: a request carries
  `state = {record, definitions}` (with the location when one is under
  evaluation), followed by the questions. `definitions` holds the record's
  record-only definitions plus those attached to this record and this
  location. A request with no matching definition is the same as before.
  `quality` evaluates the record alone, so it uses record-only definitions. Definitions are never
  truncated. A request that the definitions push over the size limit is
  refused before it is sent. Every request and its log event record the
  digest of each definition carried, and a run's triples link the run to
  them.

- **Tuning:** definitions are added in tuning, and only when they make a
  material change. The steps are:

  1. A failing or `unclear` reason names a term the record leaves undefined.
  2. A definition is written from the repository's own material and named as
     its source.
  3. The requests the definition would reach (the record's, or the record
     and location's) are run with and without it.
  4. The definition is kept only if it can change an answer: an answer's
     choice flips, or its confidence crosses the threshold that decides it.
     A move that stays on the same side of the threshold (90% to 95%) is not
     material. Candidates can be compared together, so a move that does not
     cross on its own (20% to 50%) is material when the set's combined
     change crosses. A definition that changes nothing is removed.

  The commit that adds a definition is its approval record.

- **Question naming:** a question's identity is its IRI, and an IRI is
  declared in one tree file only, across the repository: judge-jev's own trees
  and any consumer extension's (two files declaring one IRI would silently merge
  in the store). Its `jj:id`, the key in requests and reasons, is unique within
  its tree. judge-jev's questions use
  `urn:judge-jev:question:<kind>.<id>`. An extension mints its questions under
  its own namespace.

**`judge-jev doctor`** checks everything judge-jev loads in a repository and
calls nothing:
- schema validation of every tree, question set and definitions file;
- SHACL conformance to the ontology, including edges and the absence of
  cycles;
- duplicate question ids in the scope, as errors;
- warnings, without failing, for:
  - a definition with no attachment;
  - an attachment to a record the Raptor index does not have, or to a
    location that does not exist;
  - a definition whose source does not exist.

rationale.text:
Measuring a definition by its effect on Jev's answers keeps the
low-value ones out. "sc-agent" read as "a specific type of agent" may
already be inferred correctly. Targeting by record keeps every request as
small as before unless that record needs help. Definitions sourced from
the repository's own material and checked by A/B carry low risk.

positive:
Changing or removing a definition affects only the runs it reached, and
a graph query lists exactly those runs.
The A/B run spends Jev calls only on the records involved.

Orphaned definitions and dead links are found by `doctor` rather than
accumulating.
negative:
A definition is seen by every question of its record's waves, not only
the one whose reason prompted it. The A/B run compares every answer, so
an effect on another question is counted.

Consumer extensions must follow the question naming rule, or `doctor`
refuses the scope.

groups.name: One definitions file in every request
groups.description:
A repository-wide glossary sent as context with every
request.
groups.why_rejected:
At this scale it multiplies every request's size and
gives Jev unrelated material.

groups.name: Definitions inside the question text
groups.description:
Append a definition to the instructions of the question
that needed it.
groups.why_rejected:
Definitions are data, and Jev keeps data in the state.
The question text would also vary per record.

groups.name: A Raptor table now
groups.description:
Store definitions and their links in Raptor's schema
from the start.
groups.why_rejected:
The feature has to prove its value in real runs before
it gets schema space in Raptor.
